title: The End of Primacy Without Pain: Why the Domestic Foundation of American Power Is Crumbling
gist: Wertheim argues US global power rested on two domestic bargains (Cold War: high threat, high cost; post-1989: low threat, low cost) and that elites now perceive Cold War-scale threats while the public will only pay 1990s-level costs, so US foreign policy faces a widening gap that resolves through more alarm, more cost aversion, or a middle path of retrenchment plus modest spending increases.

themes.theme: Threat-cost gap in US foreign policy

insights.claim: US foreign policy is being pulled in opposite directions by rising threat perceptions among foreign-policy elites and limited cost acceptance among the voting public and political system, and this gap, present in both parties, generates policy instability beyond ordinary partisan polarization.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Expect continued sharp swings in US commitments across administrations; policy credibility risk is political, not material.
insights.quote: A chasm has opened between what American primacy demands and what American citizens will supply.
insights.locator: Mounting Burdens, Stagnant Will

insights.claim: US global power has rested on two successive domestic equilibria: high threat perception with high cost acceptance in the Cold War, and low threat perception with low cost acceptance after 1989; the post-9/11 spike faded and the system has reverted to the post-Cold War low-cost limits.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Use threat-versus-cost-acceptance as a lens for forecasting whether US defense and alliance commitments are sustainable.
insights.locator: At the outset of the Cold War, both foreign-policy elites and the general public

insights.claim: What is fracturing is not an eight-decade public attachment to a liberal rules-based order: Americans fought the Cold War because they felt threatened by communism, and since 1989 they were asked to sacrifice little for order-building.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Do not assume latent US public support for order maintenance; support was tied to threat or low cost.
insights.locator: The foreign-policy consensus is, then, breaking down

insights.claim: The domestic problem would outlast Trump even if he and his movement vanished: it stems from the post-unipolar world straining commitments against a long-standing political consensus to keep foreign policy cheap, not primarily from right-wing populism.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: A change of administration will not restore high-cost primacy; US retrenchment pressure is structural.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Overstretch arising from a political rather than material shortfall raises the risk that US commitments lose credibility and invite attacks, pushing the country into an avoidable war or an abrupt retreat.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Credibility gaps raise tail risk of conflict or sudden policy reversal in Taiwan, Baltic and Middle East theaters.
insights.locator: Mounting Burdens, Stagnant Will

insights.claim: Truman could not win congressional action on European aid with appeals to world order or humanitarianism and succeeded only by emphasizing the communist threat (the Truman Doctrine, March 1947), after which foreign policy as top problem jumped from at most 13 percent of Gallup respondents to as many as 48 percent.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Mass willingness to pay for global commitments historically required a credible, vivid threat narrative.
insights.locator: Bear Any Burden: Forging the Cold War Consensus

insights.claim: The Korean War and NSC-68 locked in high defense spending: US outlays stayed around 7 to 10 percent of GDP for two decades after the war, up from a post-WWII low of 3.5 percent in 1948.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Provides the historical benchmark of 7-10 percent of GDP against which current 3-4.5 percent budgets look modest.
insights.locator: Then, in June 1950, the Korean War broke out

insights.claim: The Soviet threat was credible because it was an expansionist great power with a universalist ideology irreconcilable with US liberal capitalism, with global stakes and a domestic fifth column fear; in 1954, 81 percent of the public saw American communists as at least some danger.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Today's adversaries lack this combination, limiting the public's willingness to mobilize.
insights.locator: Presidential salesmanship alone would not have brought about so vast a transformation

insights.claim: Roughly two-thirds of Americans in 1951-52 said keeping communism from spreading mattered more than staying out of another war, and Cold War defense spending never fell below 4.5 percent of GDP and averaged 5.6 percent in the 1980s, a level unmatched since.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of sustained cost acceptance that would be needed for a new Cold War posture.
insights.locator: Even so, in 1951 and 1952

insights.claim: After 1989 US leaders struck an unspoken compact with the public: the US would keep dominating the world so long as citizens felt almost none of the burden, justifying primacy as cheap rather than necessary.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: The post-1989 order was financed by minimal visible cost; any increase in cost tests the bargain.
insights.locator: Hardly Any Burden to Bear

insights.claim: In the 1990s the Bush Pentagon cut active-duty manpower by 25 percent and resized forces to two major regional wars while adopting aims to overmatch all conceivable adversaries; defense spending fell to 3 percent of GDP by 1999 and under 8 percent of Americans on average named foreign affairs the most important problem.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Maximalist aims were paired with falling budgets, a precedent for today's mismatch.
insights.locator: Under Presidents George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton

insights.claim: NATO enlargement succeeded because the bill appeared tiny and the pledge empty: the Pentagon estimated the US cost of admitting the first three members at only $1.5 to $2 billion over a decade by assuming a cooperative Moscow, and the Senate has near-unanimously approved all thirteen later entrants.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Alliance guarantees were ratified without informed consent for real costs; a test of Article V would expose weak domestic backing.
insights.locator: A permissive world and a passive public

themes.theme: War on terror and cost aversion

insights.claim: After 9/11 the public backed whatever cost was needed (77 percent favored retaliation even with a draft), yet Bush deferred costs through an all-volunteer force and borrowed financing; as the threat dimmed, tolerance faded despite more than 7,000 US service members killed and an estimated $8 trillion in obligations.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Public rejection of the post-9/11 wars may shape US global power more than the attacks themselves.
insights.locator: The Fading of the Forever War

insights.claim: US war deaths are now an order of magnitude below mid-twentieth-century levels: the US has lost nearly thirteen times fewer service members since the Cold War despite using force more often, with about 230 fatalities from 2014 to 2025 (3 percent of the post-Cold War total).
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Presidents of both parties avoid testing casualty tolerance, favoring standoff and airpower strategies.
insights.locator: By another common measure of cost, American war deaths

insights.claim: The war with Iran began without majority support and grew more unpopular as energy prices climbed and service members died; Trump has relied on airpower and avoided ground troops for fear of political backlash despite failing to achieve stated objectives.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Domestic cost sensitivity, including via energy prices, constrains the duration and scale of US military action in the Gulf.
insights.locator: At the time of writing, the war with Iran is a case in point

themes.theme: Defense budget numbers and public mood

insights.claim: The Commission on the National Defense Strategy called current threats the most serious since 1945 and recommended a multiple-theater force and raising defense spending from about 3 percent of GDP to 5 to 17 percent, acknowledging this would require higher taxes and entitlement cuts.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
entities: Commission on the National Defense Strategy
insights.so_what: Elite proposals imply fiscal trade-offs the political system has never accepted; treat such budget targets as aspirational.
insights.locator: One such solution came from the congressionally mandated Commission

insights.claim: The Trump administration has asked Congress to raise defense resources from $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion in fiscal 2027, about 4.5 percent of projected GDP, while Armed Services chairmen Wicker and Rogers back 5 percent of GDP.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: A $1.5 trillion request is a key test of whether the polity will fund higher threat perception; watch appropriations outcomes for defense contractors.
insights.locator: As of 2026, the Trump administration is among them

insights.claim: Despite the 2017 declaration that great power competition returned, defense spending has stayed at 3 to 3.4 percent of GDP (1990s, not 1950s, levels) and foreign-policy issues made up only about 6 percent of Gallup most-important-problem mentions from 2018 to 2024, with the share favoring an active US world role falling every year.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Public opinion data do not support a large sustained defense build-up; temper expectations of a multi-year defense supercycle.
insights.locator: In the near-decade since the 2017 U.S. National Security Strategy

insights.claim: Defense spending as a share of GDP has fallen from its twenty-first-century high of 4.7 percent in 2010, and defense spending has grown more slowly than the economy even as US policy reoriented toward major-power rivals.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Budget trend contradicts the rhetoric of mobilization.
insights.locator: Domestic Cost Aversion May Prevail

insights.claim: Moving the US onto a Cold War-like footing would likely require a genuine calamity such as a Chinese attack on Taiwan targeting US forces or Americans at home; even then a lost war could produce retrenchment or accommodation of Beijing, and an attack not targeting Americans leaves the US response uncertain given the staggering costs.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Taiwan-contingency US response is far less certain than market and alliance assumptions imply; a tail risk for semiconductors.
insights.locator: To move the U.S. political system onto a Cold War-like footing

insights.claim: Today's adversaries (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea) share no universalist ideology, have no organized US supporters, and are bound by resistance to US hegemony; Moscow failed to take Kyiv after more than four years, so the public does not perceive Cold War-scale threats, and even COVID-19 and the Ukraine invasion produced no grand transformation.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Do not expect elite threat narratives alone to drive a new US mobilization; fade risk for the defense-spending thesis.
insights.locator: But no grand transformation followed

insights.claim: US public hostility to China is softening: 28 percent of Americans called China an enemy in January 2026, down from a peak of 42 percent two years earlier, while China barely featured in the 2024 election and Trump settled for a truce after tariffs prompted Chinese critical-mineral export restrictions.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: The bipartisan China-hawk consensus may be fraying, raising odds of de-escalation episodes in US-China trade policy.
insights.locator: U.S.-China competition may be following a similar arc

insights.claim: Potential shocks accelerating US retrenchment include rising federal borrowing costs forcing a butter-over-guns choice, a foreign test of a formal US defense commitment, and younger adults, who favor a more modest military role, gaining political power.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Fiscal stress is a plausible trigger for defense-budget reprioritization; watch Treasury yields alongside defense appropriations.
insights.locator: In the future, trends could produce shocks and accelerate U.S. retrenchment

insights.claim: A middle path would shift conventional defense of Europe to Europeans, scale back Middle East entanglements, reduce Sino-American war risk (accommodation over Taiwan, Taiwan self-defense, less economic dependence on the island) and modestly raise national-security resources while avoiding a nuclear buildup; an AI-driven economic boom could fund foreign policy without changing threat perception.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Supports a base case of gradual burden-shifting to allies (European defense spending, Taiwan self-defense), with risk of gaps if executed too quickly.
insights.locator: A Middle Ground

insights.claim: The middle course faces obstacles: the US has a thin record of ending wars, accommodating rivals and shrinking alliances; rapid retrenchment opens gaps adversaries can exploit before local actors can defend themselves; and gradual retrenchment may not occur if allies slow-walk it or future presidents reverse it.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Transition periods in US alliance burden-shifting are the highest-risk windows for conflict.
insights.locator: This middle course comes with its own obstacles and drawbacks

insights.claim: Ukraine support illustrates shallow consensus: most Americans still supported Ukraine a few years in, but not intensely enough to prevent Congress from holding up aid or to elect anyone other than Trump, who pledged to broker an immediate end to the war.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Support for allies is wide but shallow; aid continuity depends on politics, not just strategy.
insights.locator: Domestic Cost Aversion May Prevail

insights.claim: The classic Lippmann gap arises when commitments exceed power; a political version of the gap, between foreign objectives and domestic will, is equally important because American power rests on the will of its people and political system as well as its resources.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Assess US strategic capacity through political willingness to pay, not only through military or economic capacity.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: America is not abandoning the post-1945 international order but seeking to revise the post-1989 arrangements and the domestic bargain that sustained them, and the paper warns against trying to restore the Kennedy-era vow to pay any price and bear any burden.
insights.speaker: Stephen Wertheim
insights.so_what: Expect selective, cost-conscious engagement rather than either withdrawal or a new Cold War.
insights.locator: America has not turned its back on the post-1945 international order
